cues.text: What We Believe
At the heart of Catholic faith stands a claim so striking that Christ's own listeners found it hard to accept.
The bread and wine offered at every Mass become, in their inmost reality, the true Body and Blood of Jesus Christ.
Not a symbol recalling him.
Not a memory of something once true.
The Lord himself, truly present, under the appearances of bread and wine.
This is the belief every account gathered in this exhibition ultimately points toward.
Before any single miracle, before any bleeding Host or vision or relic, stands this claim — old, unbroken, and resting on a foundation the Church has never had to invent.
Prepared For in the Old Covenant
Scripture opens with a God whose word does what it says.
“Let there be light,” and there was light — creation itself answers to his spoken command rather than merely describing it.
That pattern matters for understanding what Christ meant when he later said, simply, “This is my body.”
Israel's own worship had already pointed toward a meal that saves and a presence that dwells among God's people.
At the first Passover, a lamb was slain and its flesh eaten, not merely remembered, so that the angel of death would pass over each house marked by its blood.
In the desert, God fed his people with bread from heaven that they had not earned.
And at the center of the camp stood the Ark of the Covenant, carrying the manna and the tablets of the Law, the sign of God's real presence dwelling in the midst of Israel.
Christ takes up each of these threads rather than setting them aside.
He is the true Passover lamb, the bread come down from heaven, the presence that no longer rests above a mercy seat but dwells now on every altar.
The Bread of Life, and the Night He Was Betrayed
In the synagogue at Capernaum, Christ told the crowd that his flesh was true food and his blood true drink.
He did not soften the claim even as many of his own disciples turned away, unable to accept it.
He let them go rather than explain the hard saying into something easier.
On the night before he died, at a Passover meal with his apostles, he took bread, gave thanks, and said it was his body, given for them.
He did the same with the cup, calling it his blood.
Matthew, Mark, and Luke record the words, while John's Gospel presents related Eucharistic teaching in the Bread of Life discourse.
None of them softens the claim into metaphor.
Handed On, Not Invented Later
The apostles did not wait generations to grasp what they had received.
St. Paul, writing to the Corinthians only about two decades after the Last Supper — earlier than any surviving Gospel — tells them plainly that he passed on what he himself received from the Lord.
Paul goes further still.

He warns that whoever eats the bread or drinks the cup of the Lord unworthily will answer for his body and blood, and that a believer who fails to discern the body eats and drinks judgment upon himself.
This language is difficult to reconcile with reducing the Eucharist to a merely commemorative symbol.
It is the language reserved for someone truly present.
An Unbroken Witness
The principal surviving witnesses from the early Christian generations continue to affirm a strong belief in the Eucharist as more than ordinary bread and wine.
A bishop marched to execution in Rome pointed to the Eucharist as proof that Christ had come in real flesh.
A philosopher explaining the faith to a hostile emperor insisted Christians received no common bread.
A theologian countering heresies argued from the altar to the goodness of creation itself.
Centuries of Christian tradition carry this same confession forward, unbroken, long before any single miracle in this exhibition ever occurred.
Their fuller witness is worth reading on its own.
What the Miracles Are For
Every account gathered elsewhere in this exhibition is a sign offered to a faith that already stands on this older ground.
These accounts include a bleeding Host, a face seen in adoration, and hosts reported to have remained unusually well preserved.
None of them is the reason the Church believes.

They exist to help us recognize, again and again, what Scripture and the apostles and the Fathers have always taught: that Christ meant exactly what he said, and that he remains, truly, with us still.
